lessons.title: Welcome — the mental model
lessons.teaching_text: A Team Lead spawns specialist roles (executor, code-reviewer, security-reviewer, project-manager, and others) to do the actual work. Every unit of work starts life as a GitHub Discussion, gets turned into a frozen Spec, is implemented by an executor in an isolated worktree as a PR, gets reviewed, and only then merges. Nothing you haven't reviewed runs unsandboxed.

lessons.title: The role roster
lessons.teaching_text: Each role is a named agent persona with a narrow job: executor implements code from a Spec, code-reviewer inspects diffs for quality, security-reviewer audits auth/SQL/secrets-sensitive changes, project-manager writes and freezes Specs, acceptance-tester validates against the Spec, and a handful of specialists (technical-architect, product-owner, cost-analyst, performance-expert, security-expert) weigh in on Feature/Critical Discussions before a Spec is written. Team Lead is the only role that spawns others.

lessons.title: The Discussion → Spec → PR → merge loop
lessons.teaching_text: Every improvement starts as a GitHub Discussion. A consensus panel of specialists weighs in for Feature/Critical work, then project-manager freezes a Spec with runnable pass/fail acceptance criteria. An executor implements against that Spec in an isolated worktree and opens a PR. code-reviewer and (when auth/SQL/secrets are touched) security-reviewer each post a verdict; only a PR carrying all required gate labels gets merged, and the loop does that merge automatically.

lessons.title: Sandbox and worktree isolation
lessons.teaching_text: Executors and reviewers run inside a git worktree, not the parent checkout — a PreToolUse hook blocks any attempt to write to the parent repo, flip HEAD, or merge a PR from inside that isolation. This means a misbehaving or buggy agent literally cannot touch main directly; every block is logged so you can audit what was attempted.

lessons.title: Reading the dashboard
lessons.teaching_text: The dashboard surfaces what the team is doing in real time: active/recent agent runs, loop iteration history, KPI trends, and cost. Start it with scripts/start-dashboard.sh and treat it as your primary window into what's happening between check-ins rather than reading raw logs.

lessons.title: Autonomy dials
lessons.teaching_text: Autonomy is tunable per operation class (agent spawning, fast-path merges, touching external systems, self-generated idea intake), each on a 1-5 scale from manual-approval-every-time to fully autonomous. Dials default conservative and can be raised deliberately; lowering a dial takes effect immediately, raising one is a more deliberate action. Check current levels with the dial CLI before assuming a class is more or less autonomous than it is.
